questions.stem: State the energy order in which sub-shells fill from 1s through 4s.
State the four Periodic Table blocks and the criterion that assigns an element to one.
questions.modelAnswer: The s block, p block, d block and f block - named for the sub-shell holding the element's outermost electron.

questions.stem: Explain why the 4s-before-3d exception is described as energy-based rather than numeric.
questions.modelAnswer: The filling order tracks orbital energies: 3d's energy rises slightly above 4s once the third shell fills, so electrons settle into 4s first; if numbers governed the queue, 3d would precede 4s, but the observed configurations of potassium and calcium prove energy rules.

questions.stem: Predict the full configuration of an element with 19 electrons and name the block it occupies.
questions.modelAnswer: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1: the outermost electron sits in an s orbital, so the element (potassium) belongs to the s block.

Argon accounts for 18 of the 19 electrons.
Neon accounts for only 10 electrons.

options.text: A half-filled 3d5 sub-shell is energetically stable, so one 4s electron promotes

options.text: Once 3d is occupied, the 4s electrons are the outermost and easiest to remove

questions.stem: State the shorthand configuration of calcium and of the Ca2+ ion.
questions.modelAnswer: Calcium: [Ar] 4s2. Ca2+: [Ar] - after losing both 4s electrons the ion is identical to argon, matching it exactly.

questions.stem: State the anomalous configurations of chromium and copper.
questions.modelAnswer: Cr is [Ar] 3d5 4s1 (not 3d4 4s2) and Cu is [Ar] 3d10 4s1 (not 3d9 4s2) - both stabilise a half- or fully-filled 3d sub-shell.

questions.stem: Explain why writing the full configuration of gallium places 3d10 before 4s2 even though 4s filled first.
questions.modelAnswer: The full configuration lists sub-shells in numerical order for readability once 3d is occupied: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p1; the filling ORDER (4s first) describes how electrons arrived, not how the address is written.

questions.stem: Write the full configuration of the Ca2+ ion and state which neutral atom shares it.
questions.modelAnswer: Ca2+ is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 - exactly argon's configuration, identical to the noble gas, since both 4s electrons departed.

questions.stem: State what members of the same period share.
questions.modelAnswer: The same number of occupied shells - the same principal quantum number for their outer electrons.

questions.stem: State the two configuration features that make noble gases stable.
questions.modelAnswer: Full sub-shells in their electronic structures and correspondingly high ionisation energies.

questions.stem: Explain why knowing an element's block helps predict its chemistry.
questions.modelAnswer: The block names the sub-shell receiving the outermost electron, which fixes how many electrons the element typically gives, takes or shares: s-block elements lose one or two, p-block elements complete their p set, so the block is a one-glance reactivity summary.

questions.stem: Helium, neon and argon share full sub-shells. Use their configurations to explain why they appear at the end of each period.
questions.modelAnswer: Each closes its period with a complete sub-shell set - He ends 1s2, Ne ends 2p6, Ar ends 3p6 - so nothing further fits at that energy level and the next element must open a new shell, marking the period boundary.
